text:
**About 200 W of panel** gets a 1,000 Wh station back to full in roughly a day and a half of typical sun. For a full recharge in one day, you need about 270 to 340 W.

**Rule of thumb:** Divide the battery's watt-hours by 5 to get the panel wattage. A 1,000 Wh station pairs well with about 200 W of panel ([Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/)).

**Calculation:** Panel watts ≈ 1,000 ÷ (peak sun hours × 0.75). Sources use factors from 0.68 to 0.75 for real-world losses.

| Peak sun hours per day | Panel watts for a one-day recharge |
|---|---|
| 3 | about 450 W |
| 4 | about 340 W |
| 5 | about 270 W |
| 6 | about 230 W |

Sources: [Power-runtime](https://power-runtime.pages.dev/guides/solar-charging/), [Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/)

**Worked example:** A 200 W panel at 4.5 peak sun hours and 70% efficiency puts about 630 Wh into the battery per day, enough to refill 1,000 Wh in a little over a day and a half ([Watt48](https://www.watt48.com/guides/solar-panel-charging-power-station)).

**Seasonal caveat:** Winter cuts sun hours sharply. In a northern January (about 2 peak sun hours), a one-day recharge takes roughly 735 W of panel ([Held in Reserve](https://www.heldinreserve.com/power/solar-panels-recharge-power-station/)).

**Check the station's solar input limit.** Extra panel wattage does nothing above the cap. A 1,000 Wh station with a 200 W input limit will never take more than 200 W, so 200 W of panel is a sensible match. Also confirm the panel's open-circuit voltage falls within the station's input window, because exceeding it can damage the charge controller ([Enough Watts](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/how-much-solar-to-recharge); [Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/)).
